hook_text: Engineers never draw the teeth. Here is how a gear train becomes a few circles anyone can read.
clip_script: A gear on a drawing is its pitch circle, the line through the middle of the teeth, with the tooth count written beside it: 40T. Pick a scale, one millimetre per tooth, and sizes follow. Two gears that mesh have circles that just kiss, centres apart by the two radii added: 20T and 40T, 10 plus 20, 30 millimetres. Curved arrows for direction, flipping at every mesh. Add an idler in the middle and the ends turn the same way; label it, and the ratio stays. Draw 12T driving 48T: four to one, slow and strong, your winder. Swap the labels so 48T drives: one to four, fast and weak, a hand drill. Same circles, different driver, different machine. Write the ratio, the MA and which gear drives, put the scale in the title block, and your sheet is a drawing an engineer can build from.
visual_style: Compass draws two kissing circles on a whiteboard sheet; 20T and 40T labels and alternating arrows appear; a third circle slides in as an idler; 12T/48T pair with driver label swapping sides and the ratio flipping.
pacing: The convention, the pair, the idler, slow and fast, the notes.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw your team's winder train as pitch circles with tooth counts.
